content.title: About
content.content: The multigrain bagel is a yeasted baked good that incorporates whole grains, bran, and seeds (sunflower, pumpkin, flax). It has the classic round shape with a hole in the middle, a dense crumb and a slightly crisp crust. Bagels are often sliced, toasted, and topped with cream cheese, hummus, or used as a sandwich base.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bagels originated in Eastern European Jewish cuisine and became popular in the United States in the early 20th century.
Traditional preparation involves boiling the dough briefly in water with baking soda before baking, which gives the bagel its distinctive chew.
The multigrain version appeared in the 1970s as a response to growing demand for more nutritious, whole‑grain products.
In many countries the bagel is considered a "grab‑and‑go" breakfast because it is easy to eat on the move.
There are over 30 bagel varieties, ranging from raisin and cranberry to cheese and seed‑topped versions.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Whole grains and bran increase dietary fiber, supporting healthy digestion.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Slow‑digesting carbohydrates provide steady energy and help keep you full longer.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: Sunflower and pumpkin seeds add polyunsaturated fatty acids that are beneficial for heart health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Grain components are rich in thiamine, niacin, and folate, which are important for metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The bagel supplies magnesium, iron and zinc, essential for muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Seed allergy
items.content: Sunflower, pumpkin or flax seeds may trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: High sodium
items.content: Some bagels are topped with coarse salt; people watching sodium intake should choose unsalted versions.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Made from wheat flour, bagels contain gluten and are not suitable for those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Added seeds and bran can make the bagel more calorie‑dense than plain bread; moderation is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice the bagel in half, toast it, and spread cream cheese, avocado, hummus or peanut butter. It works well as a sandwich with turkey, smoked salmon, vegetables and greens. Small bagel cubes can be added to salads or used as a crunchy topping for soups.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the bagel in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer storage, refrigerate (up to 7 days) or freeze (up to 3 months). Before eating, warm it in a toaster or oven to restore the crisp crust.

content.title: About
content.content: Bread is a staple food made by baking a dough of flour, water, yeast and salt. Spanish coffee is a fragrant beverage prepared from roasted Arabica beans, often served as espresso or "café con leche".

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional Spanish bread "pan" often has a crunchy crust and a soft crumb.
In Spain, "café con leche" and "café solo" are popular and served in small cups.
Spanish coffee plantations are located in the Canary Islands, where the climate suits Arabica cultivation.
Mediterranean breads are frequently enriched with olive oil and rosemary.
Coffee in Spain is commonly accompanied by sweet pastries such as churros.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Bread provides a quick supply of carbohydrates, while coffee stimulates metabolism thanks to caffeine.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Especially whole‑grain flour contains vitamins B1, B3 and B6, important for the nervous system.

items.title: Antioxidants in coffee
items.content: Coffee contains polyphenols that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Caffeine speeds intestinal motility, and whole‑grain bread supplies dietary fiber.

items.title: Improves concentration
items.content: Caffeine enhances alertness and cognitive performance.

items.title: Gluten sensitivity
items.content: People with celiac disease or gluten intolerance may experience serious symptoms from bread.

items.title: Excess caffeine intake
items.content: High doses of coffee can cause anxiety, insomnia and rapid heartbeat.

items.title: Sugar and salt content
items.content: Some breads and ready‑to‑drink coffee beverages contain added sugar and salt, which is undesirable for hypertension.

items.title: Acidity of coffee
items.content: The acidic nature of coffee may irritate the stomach in individuals with gastritis or ulcers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Bread can be enjoyed fresh, toasted, as sandwiches, or used in recipes. Spanish coffee is typically served hot as espresso, "café con leche" or "café americano". Pair bread with olive oil, cheese, ham or sweet spreads, and coffee with desserts such as churros.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store bread in a cool, dry place in a paper bag or bread box to keep the crust crisp. For longer storage, freeze bread in an airtight bag. Keep coffee in a sealed container away from light, moisture and heat; a dark pantry is ideal.

chicken-breast-stewed-skin-not-eaten.title: Chicken Breast, Stewed, Skin Not Eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Stewed chicken breast without skin is a lean source of protein obtained by slowly simmering the meat in a small amount of liquid. The cooking method retains most nutrients, yields tender meat, and is easy to digest.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken breast contains very little fat, especially when the skin is removed.
Stewing helps preserve moisture and flavor, making the meat softer than when it is fried.
Chicken is one of the most affordable complete protein sources worldwide.
Different cuisines use various herbs, spices, and vegetables for stewing, creating diverse flavor profiles.
Stewed chicken breast is a staple in diet plans and athletic nutrition.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: A 100‑g serving provides about 31 g of high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Without skin, fat content is under 2 g per 100 g, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken breast supplies niacin (B3), vitamin B6, and small amounts of B12, supporting energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It contains phosphorus, selenium and zinc, important for bones, immune function and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Easily digestible
items.content: The soft texture of stewed meat makes it gentle on the stomach.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Undercooked chicken may harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter; cook to an internal temperature of 75 °C.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: A small number of people can experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Adding salt or pre‑made sauces can raise sodium levels, which is a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Vitamin loss with prolonged cooking
items.content: Some water‑soluble vitamins, such as B6, may degrade during long stewing periods.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Stewed chicken breast can be sliced and served as a main dish, added to salads, soups, stews, pasta, or used in sandwiches. It can also be diced and frozen for quick future meals.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the cooked meat to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags for 2‑3 months. Reheat thoroughly before consumption.

content.title: About
content.content: EAS Soy Protein Powder (item 5485) is a high‑quality nutritional mix containing soy protein isolate, vitamins and minerals. It is formulated to support muscle growth, post‑workout recovery and to provide the body with essential nutrients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Contains more than 90 % pure soy protein.
Enriched with B‑vitamins, vitamin D and calcium for metabolism and bone health.
Free from lactose, gluten and artificial colourings.
Suitable for vegetarians and vegans.
Produced using cold‑extraction technology, preserving protein bioactivity.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: Helps repair and build muscle tissue after physical activity.

items.title: Low fat level
items.content: Supports calorie‑controlled diets, useful for weight management.

items.title: Rich in vitamins and minerals
items.content: B‑vitamins, D and calcium aid energy metabolism, bone strength and immunity.

items.title: Cardiovascular support
items.content: Soy protein contains isoflavones that may help maintain healthy cholesterol levels.

items.title: Convenient to use
items.content: Easily dissolves in water, milk or plant‑based drinks for a quick nutritious shake.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to soy may experience reactions up to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Phytoestrogens
items.content: Soy isoflavones have mild estrogenic activity; consult a doctor if you have hormonal disorders.

items.title: Excessive protein intake
items.content: Very high protein consumption can strain the kidneys, especially in people with chronic kidney disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Mix 30 g of powder with 250–300 ml of water, milk or a plant‑based beverage. It can also be added to smoothies, oatmeal or baked goods to boost protein content.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place in a tightly sealed container. For long‑term storage, keep refrigerated to prevent moisture absorption.

pasta-with-cream-sauce-and-meat-ready-to.title: Pasta with Cream Sauce and Meat, Ready-to-Heat

content.title: About
content.content: Pasta with cream sauce and meat is a ready‑to‑heat meal that stays refrigerated and requires only a short reheating. It contains pasta, a smooth cream sauce, and tender pieces of cooked meat, seasoned with herbs and spices. The dish is designed for a quick, tasty lunch or dinner.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The meal is engineered for convenience: just 2‑3 minutes in a microwave or on the stovetop.
The cream sauce is made from dairy cream and a small amount of flour, giving it a silky texture.
Meat is usually chicken or turkey, making the product lower in fat than beef‑based versions.
The pasta is often fortified with B‑vitamins and iron to support energy levels.
Packaging is microwave‑safe, eliminating the need to transfer to another dish.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: The meat provides a complete set of essential amino acids needed for tissue repair.

items.title: Energy supply
items.content: Carbohydrates from the pasta deliver a quick source of energy, ideal for busy days.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: The cream sauce contributes calcium for bone health, while vitamin D aids its absorption.

items.title: Iron content
items.content: Meat adds iron, which is crucial for oxygen transport in the blood.

items.title: Portion control
items.content: A single ready‑to‑heat package offers a defined portion, helpful for diet management.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Ready meals often contain higher salt; people with hypertension should limit intake.

items.title: Allergen presence
items.content: The cream sauce may trigger reactions in individuals with dairy allergies.

items.title: Trans fats
items.content: Some formulations may contain small amounts of trans fats, which should be minimized.

items.title: Shelf life after opening
items.content: Once opened, keep the product refrigerated and consume within 2‑3 days.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the meal in the microwave for about 2‑3 minutes, stirring halfway to ensure even warming of the sauce. Alternatively, heat on the stovetop, stirring continuously. For extra flavor, add fresh herbs, grated cheese, or vegetables.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened package in the refrigerator at 0 °C – +4 °C. After opening, reseal tightly or transfer to an airtight container and keep refrigerated. Do not freeze, as the sauce texture may change.

content.title: About
content.content: Pasta with cream sauce is a home recipe where cooked noodles are coated with a smooth sauce made from cream, cheese, garlic and spices. The dish is quick to prepare, has a mild creamy flavor and works well for lunch or dinner.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cream sauce is often made with 20 % cream and grated Parmesan, giving it a distinctive aroma.
In Italy pasta is traditionally served "al dente", slightly firm in the center, so the sauce adheres better.
Making the sauce at home allows better control of taste and salt content compared to store‑bought packets.
Variations may include mushrooms, ham or spinach for a richer flavor profile.
The cream used in the sauce is rich in fatty acids, which, in moderation, contribute to satiety.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Cream and cheese in the sauce provide calcium, essential for bone and tooth health.

items.title: Energy‑dense
items.content: Pasta supplies complex carbohydrates while the cream sauce adds fats, making the meal calorie‑rich and satisfying.

items.title: Contains vitamin D
items.content: Enriched cream can be a source of vitamin D, which aids calcium absorption.

items.title: Supports nervous system
items.content: B‑vitamins present in pasta help maintain normal nervous system function.

items.title: Enhances flavor perception
items.content: Fats in the cream sauce amplify aromas and taste, making the dish more enjoyable.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The cream sauce is rich in fat, so the dish can be high‑calorie and may not suit strict diets.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Cream and cheese may cause discomfort for people who are lactose intolerant.

items.title: Milk allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to dairy should avoid the cream sauce.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Adding a lot of cheese or using a prepared sauce can raise the salt content, which is undesirable for hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cook the pasta until al dente. In a separate pan heat the cream, add grated Parmesan, minced garlic, salt and pepper, and stir until the sauce is smooth. Drain the pasta, combine it with the sauce and heat for 1‑2 minutes so the noodles are fully coated.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared sauce in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Pasta is best served immediately, but can be kept in the fridge for up to 2 days, reheating with a splash of cream or water.

content.title: About
content.content: Salisbury steak is a seasoned ground beef patty shaped like a steak and served with a rich brown gravy made from beef broth, onions, carrots, and tomato paste. The dish originated in the United States in the early 20th century and became popular for its hearty flavor and ease of preparation.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name “Salisbury steak” comes from Dr. James H. Salisbury, a 19th‑century physician who promoted minced beef as a health food.
Traditional gravy is thickened with a roux of butter and flour, giving it a smooth, velvety texture.
In the U.S. it is commonly served with mashed potatoes or egg noodles, while in the UK it is sometimes called a “ground beef steak”.
There are many sauce variations, from classic brown gravy to tomato‑wine mushroom sauces.
Salisbury steak is a staple in school cafeterias and military mess halls because it is nutritious and inexpensive.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Ground beef provides a complete source of high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Red meat contains heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Salisbury steak supplies vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Calcium from gravy
items.content: When dairy or fortified broth is used in the gravy, the dish adds extra calcium.

items.title: Low in carbs
items.content: The meal is suitable for low‑carbohydrate diets when served without starchy sides.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Ground beef can be high in saturated fats, which should be limited in heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: Sodium in gravy
items.content: Gravy often contains added salt or soy sauce, increasing overall sodium intake.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Improper cooking of ground beef can lead to salmonella or E. coli contamination.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: Some individuals may have an allergy or intolerance to beef.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Shape the seasoned ground beef into 2‑3 cm thick patties, sear them on high heat until browned, then simmer in the gravy for 15–20 minutes until cooked through. For the gravy, sauté onions and carrots, stir in flour, then add beef broth, tomato paste, and seasonings. Serve with mashed potatoes, rice, or a vegetable side.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked Salisbury steak in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 75 °C to ensure safety.

stuffed-cabbage-with-meat-puerto-rican-s.title: Stuffed cabbage with meat, Puerto Rican style

content.title: About
content.content: Stuffed cabbage with meat, Puerto Rican style is a classic dish of Puerto Rican cuisine that consists of cabbage leaves wrapped around a mixture of ground beef, pork, rice, tomatoes, onion, and characteristic spices such as adobo, oregano, and cumin. It is simmered in a fragrant tomato‑based broth until the cabbage is tender.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish blends Spanish colonial culinary heritage with local Caribbean flavors.
In Puerto Rico cabbage is often used instead of traditional banana leaves, making the recipe more accessible.
Stuffed cabbage is commonly served at holidays and family celebrations as a symbol of abundance.
The rice in the filling is usually toasted first to keep it fluffy after cooking.
Traditional sauce may contain a splash of vinegar, giving the dish a subtle tang.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: The meat filling provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef and pork supply vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Fiber from cabbage and rice
items.content: Cabbage leaves and whole‑grain rice aid digestion and promote satiety.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Tomatoes and spices (adobo, oregano) are rich in antioxidants that combat free radicals.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The dish contains iron, zinc, and potassium, important for immune function and blood pressure regulation.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: The sauce often includes added salt and soy sauce, so people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Meat fat
items.content: Pork can be fatty; lean cuts or reduced amounts can be used for a lighter version.

items.title: Spice allergy
items.content: Some spices (e.g., cumin) may trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Tomato acidity
items.content: Tomatoes increase acidity, which may be problematic for those with ulcer disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot, garnished with fresh cilantro or parsley. A squeeze of lime adds brightness. It pairs well with rice, beans, or crusty bread.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat gently on the stove or in the microwave, adding a splash of broth to prevent drying out.

content.title: About
content.content: Tangerine is a small sweet citrus fruit (Citrus reticulata) native to Southeast Asia. It has a bright orange peel, juicy flesh, and a distinctive aroma. Tangerines are usually eaten fresh but are also used in juices, desserts, and various culinary dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tangerines belong to the same family as oranges, lemons, and limes.
There are more than 150 tangerine varieties, differing in size, taste, and peel color.
The name “tangerine” comes from the Chinese Ming dynasty, during which the fruit was first exported to Europe.
The peel is rich in essential oils that are used in aromatherapy and perfumery.
In Chinese culture, tangerines are a symbol of luck and prosperity, especially during the New Year.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Tangerines are an excellent source of vitamin C, which supports the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains flavonoids
items.content: Flavonoids in tangerines have antioxidant properties that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: The fiber in tangerines promotes regular bowel movements and helps prevent constipation.

items.title: Provides potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports normal blood pressure.

items.title: Low‑calorie snack
items.content: Tangerines are relatively low in calories, making them a good choice for weight management.

items.title: Citrus allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to tangerines, including skin rash, swelling, or breathing difficulties.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The high acidity can irritate the stomach lining in people with gastritis or ulcer disease.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: The natural fructose may be a concern for people with diabetes; portion control is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Tangerines are typically eaten fresh by cutting them in half and pulling apart the segments. They can be added to salads, yogurts, cereals, baked goods, or used as an ingredient in juices and smoothies.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store tangerines in the refrigerator’s fruit drawer, where they stay fresh for 2‑3 weeks. At room temperature they lose aroma quickly and become softer.

turkey-light-or-dark-meat-fried-coated-s.title: Turkey, light or dark meat, fried, coated, skin not eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Turkey is a large bird native to North America. The meat can be light (breast) or dark (thighs, drumsticks). This product consists of turkey pieces that are coated and deep‑fried, with the skin removed before cooking.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turkeys were domesticated by Native Americans over 2,000 years ago.
Light meat contains less fat than dark meat, but both are high‑quality protein sources.
Deep‑frying creates a crispy crust while the coating locks in juices.
Turkey skin is often discarded for this preparation because it can become tough when fried.
In the United States turkey is strongly associated with Thanksgiving.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: A 100 g serving of fried turkey provides about 25 g of high‑quality protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Turkey contains virtually no carbs, making it suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The meat supplies niacin, vitamin B6 and vitamin B12, which support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It provides iron, zinc and phosphorus, important for blood formation and bone health.

items.title: Lower cholesterol than red meat
items.content: Although frying adds fat, turkey generally has lower cholesterol than beef.

items.title: High fat and calorie content from frying
items.content: Deep‑frying increases calories and saturated fat, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to bird meat.

items.title: Risk of bacterial contamination
items.content: Undercooked turkey can harbor pathogens such as Salmonella.

items.title: Sodium in the coating
items.content: Pre‑made breadings often contain added salt; choose low‑sodium versions if you monitor sodium intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve fried coated turkey as a main dish, in salads, with sauces, or in sandwiches. Pair it with vegetable sides or whole‑grain products for a balanced meal.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked fried turkey in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in bags at –18 °C, where it retains quality for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C before eating.
